title: Who wrote what
hook: scholars debate the authorship of some letters; churches receive them all as scripture
tomorrow: why do some lines in Paul's letters suddenly sound like a song?

segments.voice: Jude's stormy letter ended in a doxology, praise to the one able to keep you from falling. The letters with names on them are nearly read through. So whose names are they?
screen: `ABLE TO KEEP YOU.` → `WHOSE NAMES ARE THESE?`

segments.voice: A grandmother's hands shake too much to type, so she talks and her granddaughter types. Tell your uncle the roses came up. At the bottom, before sending, the granddaughter slips in a line of her own: hi, it's me typing. Near the end of Romans, the very same thing happens. In the middle of Paul's greetings, a new voice breaks in: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." All along, a reader might assume Paul held the pen. He didn't.
screen: `SHE TALKS, YOU TYPE.` → `HI, IT'S ME TYPING.` → `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS EPISTLE.`

segments.voice: Once you notice Tertius, the letters start showing their workshop. In Galatians, Paul takes the pen near the end: "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand." In Second Thessalonians he calls his handwritten greeting "the token in every epistle." First Peter says it was written "By Silvanus, a faithful brother." Hebrews never names its writer at all. So a letter could have a sender, a scribe, co-senders in the first line, and a signature at the bottom. Some scholars go a step further. They ask whether a few letters that carry Paul's or Peter's name were written later by followers, in the teacher's name. Other scholars hold that each letter comes from the one it names. That's a real debate, and it's still going. Meanwhile, churches kept reading every one of these letters aloud as scripture. Second Peter already talks that way about Paul. It says his letters hold "some things hard to be understood," which some people twist, "as they do also the other scriptures." Other scriptures: Paul's mail, set beside the holy books. A letter's place never hung on whose hand held the pen. It hung on being received.
screen: `TERTIUS HOLDS THE PEN.` · `SENDERS, SCRIBES, SIGNATURES.` · `A REAL DEBATE ABOUT NAMES.` · `SET BESIDE THE OTHER SCRIPTURES.` · then, large: `RECEIVED AS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Open any one of the letters to its first verse, on a phone or a page, and look only at the names: who it's from, who it's to, and whether more than one sender stands in that first line. Then rest your eyes on the page for the sit. Someone wrote this to someone, and it reached you.
Who wrote what. The question the letters raise themselves, with a scribe like Tertius, co-senders, and a signature in the writer's own hand.
Pocket this one: received as scripture, whoever's hand held the pen and whatever name sat at the top. Day fifteen ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 1597 COUNTS.` → `THE LETTERS, READ THROUGH · 66 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DO SOME LINES IN PAUL'S LETTERS SOUND LIKE A SONG?`

howItsDone: Churches read the New Testament letters aloud in worship as scripture, often announced by the name the letter carries, as in 'a reading from the letter of Paul to the Romans.'

fork.setup: your church newsletter prints a letter 'from the pastor,' but you know the office manager typed it from his notes. a friend says that makes it fake. what do the New Testament letters suggest?
options: it's fake; only handwritten letters really count.
a letter can have a scribe and still be the sender's.
it belongs to the office manager now.
fork.reveal: Tertius wrote Romans down, 1 Peter was written 'by Silvanus', and Paul signed in his own hand. senders and scribes worked together, and the letters stayed the senders'.

original.note: Greek: I write. Paul's "so I write" in 2 Thessalonians 3:17, under his own signature.

chat.says: found grandma's old letters in pop's boxes. one's in aunt jo's writing. grandma dictated it. still grandma's letter?
options: Yes. Tertius held the pen for Romans, and it's still Paul's. Her words, kept and read.
Not really. A letter is only truly hers if every word is in her own handwriting.
It's Aunt Jo's now. Whoever holds the pen is the real writer, so it's her letter.
chat.meaning: Romans had a scribe, Tertius, and stayed Paul's letter. A letter's place came from whose words it carried and from being received and read.

Tertius.meaning: the scribe who wrote Romans down and added his own hello

Galatians.meaning: Paul's letter to the churches of Galatia

Silvanus.meaning: the faithful brother named at the close of First Peter

Hebrews.meaning: a New Testament letter that never names its writer

epistle.meaning: the King James word for a letter
